summary:
Côte d'Ivoire does not criminalise same-sex conduct. The US State Department's 2023 country report on human rights practices states that same-sex relations are not an offence, so a trans visitor carries no statutory exposure on that ground. The sources assembled here do not cover entry, visa or identity-document screening rules specific to transgender travellers.

Non-state violence against LGBTQ people is documented and has been lethal. The 2023 report records three deaths within the community during that year. Police responses to violence committed by non-state actors were described as sometimes slow and ineffective and often blaming the victim, although authorities were handling complaints somewhat better than in previous years.

Gender-nonconforming people face the sharper risk. A transgender man was beaten in Abobo, a district of Abidjan, while walking with another man. Academic research on Ivoirian travestis reports harsher stigmatisation and violence than that experienced by sexual minorities whose gender presentation avoids attention, alongside social exclusion and isolation, some of it traced to the 2010-11 post-election violence.

Protection machinery exists on paper. A UNDP report of December 2024, marking ten years of African Commission Resolution 275, includes a Côte d'Ivoire overview assessing the protective legal environment, investigation and prosecution of perpetrators, access to justice, civic space, and inclusion of LGBT+ people. Human Rights Watch's Côte d'Ivoire country page lists LGBT Rights only as a topic facet, without publishing a case or report on the housing of transgender prisoners: where trans detainees are placed, whether dedicated units exist, and whether solitary confinement or segregation is used are not covered in any listed publication.
tangentialFactors:
The 2011 US State Department human rights report for Côte d'Ivoire, covering the post-electoral crisis, records roughly 3,000 deaths, sexual violence and mass displacement. That report contains limited LGBT-specific content, but the wider instability it documents forms part of the context in which the 2015 research on travestis situates heightened isolation.

A New York Times article of October 2024 addresses the situation of LGBTQ people in Côte d'Ivoire, indicating continued press attention to the issue beyond the official reporting cycle.
localsOnly:
Ivoirian rights groups have been criticised for distancing themselves from travestis, leaving that population underserved relative to other sexual minorities, according to the 2015 study in Critical African Studies by Thomann and Corey-Boulet. The same research documents resilience alongside violence and social exclusion.

Authorities were reported to be handling complaints somewhat better than in previous years, per the 2023 State Department report, even as police responses to non-state violence remained slow, ineffective and prone to blaming the victim.
outOfScopeNotes:
Entry, visa and identity-document screening rules specific to transgender travellers are not covered by the sources assembled here; this remains unresolved rather than confirmed absent.

Placement of transgender detainees, the existence of dedicated units, and use of solitary confinement or segregation are not sourced in any listed publication, including Human Rights Watch's Côte d'Ivoire material. The UNDP country overview's specific findings on investigation, prosecution and access to justice are referenced only at the level of the report's stated scope; the underlying assessments are not reproduced in the inventory.
